text: section: Origins & Folk Tradition content: The temple's history stretches back several centuries and is rooted in oral tradition rather than written records. According to popular tradition, Komaranna, a devotee from the Yadava community, performed deep penance (tapas) for Lord Shiva on this hilltop. Lord Shiva appeared before him as Mallanna, and Komaranna installed the divine 8-foot clay idol on the hill, establishing the shrine. A separate popular legend holds that Lord Mallikarjuna appeared in a dream to a shepherd and told him he was enshrined on Indrakeeladri hill in 'Putta Matti' (soft earth) to fulfill devotees' desires. The current clay idol is believed to be ~500 years old. Worship of Mallanna originally flourished among shepherds, farmers and warriors, and over time the site transformed into a major pilgrimage centre attracting devotees from across Telangana. As the rush of devotees increased, the temple committee (and later the Endowments Department) renovated the temple complex, built mandapams, choultries, rest rooms, water facilities, and the 200+ room accommodation block. The Mallanna story has no written script — it is preserved and sung in the Oggu Katha folk-narrative tradition by the Oggu community. foundation year: Several centuries (oral tradition); clay idol estimated ~500 years old founders: Folk tradition attributes the temple's origin to Komaranna, a devotee from the Yadava community (per Travelshexa, Xploring Destinations) Later patronised by regional rulers and the Telangana Endowments Department legends: Komaranna from the Yadava community performed penance; Lord Shiva appeared as Mallanna and was installed as the 8-foot clay idol on the hilltop. Lord Mallikarjuna appeared in a dream to a shepherd, saying he was enshrined on Indrakeeladri in 'Putta Matti' to fulfill devotees' desires. The Mallanna story has no written script — it is preserved in the Oggu Katha folk-narrative tradition. In the Oggu Katha, Swamy Mallanna marries goddess Medalamma by facing conditions set by her brothers; Medalamma is also called Bramarambika, consort of Lord Shiva. The Yadava and Linga Balija communities head all important rituals in turn as a matter of sentiment (Yadava for Golla Kethamma, Balija for Medalamma). section: Renovation & Modern Administration content: As the devotee rush increased, the temple committee started developmental activities, and later the Telangana Endowments Department renovated the temple complex, constructed mandapams, choultries, rest rooms and water facilities. A 200+ room accommodation block was made available for pilgrims by the Komuravelli Devasthanam Board. The Sri Mallikarjuna Swamy Devasthanam Board also enabled online reservations for various pujas, offerings, annadanam and sevas. The deity is 'coloured' (annually re-painted/re-decorated) once a year. The complex is distinguished by its yellow paint — the colour used to mark buildings registered as temple property. legends: Endowments Department renovated mandapams and choultries; ~200 rooms for devotees' accommodation by the Devasthanam Board. Temple and rooms are painted in yellow to mark them as registered temple property. The deity is 'coloured' (annually re-decorated) once a year.

text: Lord Mallanna, the Telangana folk-form of Lord Shiva, is revered as a guardian deity (Grama Devata) of villages, livestock and the rural poor. According to popular tradition, Komaranna of the Yadava community performed intense penance on Indrakeeladri hill, and Lord Shiva appeared before him as Mallanna. Komaranna installed the 8-foot clay idol, which remains the presiding deity. Mallanna's story — unwritten and transmitted orally — is performed in the Oggu Katha by hereditary singer-storytellers (the Oggu community), who narrate his exploits and his marriage to the goddess Medalamma after overcoming the conditions set by her brothers. Devotees believe Mallanna hears prayers directly and delivers immediate justice, mediating land, legal and family conflicts.

text: Mallanna is at the heart of Telangana's folk devotion, embodying faith, social justice and community bonding that bridges castes and classes. He is seen as a champion of justice and truth, a mediator for land, legal and family conflicts, a protector of villages and livestock, and a vanquisher of fear, evil spirits and negative energies. Devotees regard him as a 'living god' who hears prayers directly without intermediaries. He is especially popular among the Kuruma, Mudhiraj, Yadava and other BC communities. The temple is one of the prominent Shiva shrines in northern Telangana, alongside Vemulawada (Rajarajeshwara) and Kaleshwaram (Mukteshwara).

text: The temple is believed to be a sacred spot for instant justice and divine protection. Devotees come seeking help with health issues, court cases, family concerns and land disputes. Unlike classical Agama temples, worship here is heartfelt, emotional and woven into everyday rural life, expressed through folk offerings and vows rather than formal paid rituals. All mantras are chanted in Telugu (not Sanskrit) — a distinctive inclusive tradition that sets this temple apart from most major Indian shrines.

text: The temple is built in a simple folk-temple style (no towering gopurams) and is located in a cave on the Indrakeeladri hillock, reached by a short climb of about 100 steps. The main sanctum houses Lord Mallanna in a humble folk style as a seated 8-foot clay murti in 'vigraha rupam' (statue form) rather than the more common 'linga rupam'. The complex includes a Medalamma (consort) sannidhi, subsidiary shrines for Ganesha, Nandi and the Navagrahas (on an elevated platform), and a Veera Bhadra cave temple (with a sacred Shiva Linga and Nandi) reached by climbing a few more steps. There are separate passages for entrance and exit from the cave temple. The main entrance tower, compound wall, Mukhamantapa and cottages are painted in yellow to mark them as temple property. The complex has a spacious open courtyard for large gatherings, and ~200 rooms for devotees' accommodation managed by the Devasthanam Board.

text: Mondays, Sundays and Amavasya days are the principal weekly occasions for Mallanna worship. The Sankranti-to-Ugadi Jathara season is the most vibrant but most crowded. For the Jathara atmosphere without overwhelming crowds, a mid-Jathara Sunday (around the 5th–6th week, ~20,000–30,000 devotees) is the best compromise versus the peak first/last Sundays (50,000–100,000). Avoid peak Jathara days if you dislike crowds. Early weekday mornings are best for peaceful, crowd-free darshan.

text:
Question: Who do people worship at Komuravelli Temple?
Answer: The temple is dedicated to Lord Mallanna (Mallikarjuna Swamy), a revered folk representation of Lord Shiva appearing in 'vigraha rupam' (murti) form, with consorts Golla Kethamma (Yadava community) and Medalamma / Bramarambika (Linga Balija community). He is also venerated as Khandoba by Maharashtrian devotees.

text: Alternate names: Edupayala Temple Sri Vana Durga Bhavani Temple Edupayala Durga Bhavani Temple Edupayalamma Temple Edupayala Durgamma Devasthanam Alternate spellings: Edupayala Yedupayala Edu Payalu Vana Durga Bhavani Edupayalamma Nagasanpally / Nagasanipally Presiding deity: Goddess Sri Vana Durga Bhavani (Edupayalamma) — a Swayambhu (self-manifested) forest-form of Goddess Durga, enshrined in the sanctum in the middle of the Manjeera River where it splits into seven streams Other deities: Lord Shiva (smaller shrine) Lord Ganesha (smaller shrine) Other Hindu deities Sri Edupayala Vana Durga Bhavani Temple (Sri Edupayala Vana Durga Bhavani Devasthanam), popularly known as Edupayala Temple, is one of the most revered Swayambhu Shakti temples in Telangana. Located at Nagasanpally village, Papannapet Mandal, Medak district, the temple sits in the middle of the Manjeera River, where it splits into seven distinct streams — hence the name 'Edupayala' (Telugu 'Edu' = seven, 'Payalu' = streams). Per some traditions, the seven streams are named after the seven great sages: Jamadagni, Atri, Kasyapa, Viswamitra, Vasistha, Bharadwaja and Gautama. The presiding deity is Goddess Vana Durga Bhavani (Edupayalamma), a forest-form of Goddess Durga who is believed to be self-manifested (Swayambhu) in a den ('Pedda Gutta Soramgam' / 'Garuda Ganga'). The complex is administered by the Telangana Endowments Department under a non-hereditary Trust Board, with A. Chandrasekhar as the Executive Officer. The annual Edupayala Jatara, celebrated around Maha Shivaratri (Feb/Mar), is a State Festival of Telangana and one of the state's largest religious gatherings. Every year ~30 lakh devotees visit; the three-day Jatara draws 5+ lakh pilgrims. During the monsoon, the seven swollen rivulets flow around and reach the feet of the Goddess — an event considered highly auspicious and at times severe enough to submerge the temple (as in August–October 2025, when the temple was underwater for 50+ days due to Singur dam releases).

text: section: Origin & Parikshit / Janamejaya Legend content: The temple is believed to have been established in the 12th century and has remained an important centre of Shakti worship ever since. The presiding deity is Goddess Vana Durga (a forest form of Durga), who is believed to be self-manifested (Swayambhu) in a den (Pedda Gutta Soramgam, also called Garuda Ganga). A popular legend links the seven streams to the Mahabharata: King Janamejaya (son of Maharaja Parikshit, grandson of Arjuna) performed the Sarpa Yagna to avenge his father's death by snakebite. During the ritual, when Garuda carried away the sacrificial snakes, drops of their blood (per some versions) — or the spirit of Ganga (per other versions) — fell at seven different places, forming the seven streams that converge at Edupayala before joining the Manjeera River. Some traditions specifically name the streams after the seven great sages: Jamadagni, Atri, Kasyapa, Viswamitra, Vasistha, Bharadwaja and Gautama. Per temple tradition, the Goddess's idol was discovered in a den on the way to the temple, and the seven streams are said to touch the feet of the Goddess at the point where they merge. foundation year: 12th century (per local tradition; clay/Swayambhu idol discovered in the den) founders: Per popular legend: Komaranna/Yadava devotees (no historical record; pre-12th century oral tradition) legends: Goddess Vana Durga is Swayambhu — her idol was discovered in a den ('Pedda Gutta Soramgam' / 'Garuda Ganga') on the way to the temple. Per the Mahabharata-linked legend, during King Janamejaya's (or his father Parikshit's) Sarpa Yagna, Garuda carried away the sacrificial snakes, and drops of blood (or the spirit of Ganga, per other versions) fell at seven places, forming the seven streams that converge at Edupayala. The seven streams are named after the seven great sages (Saptarishis): Jamadagni, Atri, Kasyapa, Viswamitra, Vasistha, Bharadwaja and Gautama (per temple tradition). The streams begin their journey from the Ghanpur project and meet again just behind the sanctum, where the Goddess is enshrined. section: Nizam Period & Modern Administration content: Per the Wikipedia article on Papannapet, the temple's maintenance was under family members of Peddalachannagari's during the Nizam's rule. Peddalachannagai Durga Reddy was the first chairman of the temple Trust board. In 2015, the Telangana government constituted non-hereditary Trust Boards for 19 major temples under the AP Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act 1987 (Telangana Adaptation order 2014); Sri Edupayala Vana Durga Bhavani Temple (Nagasanipally village, Papannapet Mandal, Medak District) was named as one of the 16 major temples with annual income above Rs 1 crore. The Edupayala Jatara was accorded the status of a State Festival. The current Executive Officer (as of 2025) is A. Chandrasekhar. In 2025, the temple was submerged for 50+ days due to heavy monsoon rain combined with massive releases from the Singur project (nearly one lakh cusecs); property loss was preliminarily estimated at ₹1 crore, and the Navaratri celebrations were held for the first time atop the flooded structure. founders: Peddalachannagai Durga Reddy — first chairman of the temple Trust board (during/after the Nizam period) legends: Temple maintenance was under family members of Peddalachannagari's during the Nizam's rule. 2015: Constituted as a non-hereditary Trust Board under the Telangana Endowments Department (one of 19 major temples). Edupayala Jatara was recognised as a State Festival of Telangana. August–October 2025: Temple submerged for 50+ days due to Singur project releases; property loss estimated at ₹1 crore; Navaratri 2025 held for the first time atop the flooded structure.

Per the Mahabharata-linked legend, during King Janamejaya's Sarpa Yagna, Garuda carried away the sacrificial snakes, and drops of blood (or the spirit of Ganga, per other versions) fell at seven different places, forming the seven streams that converge at the temple before joining the Manjeera River. Per local tradition, the Goddess's idol was discovered in a den ('Pedda Gutta Soramgam' / 'Garuda Ganga') on the way to the temple, sanctifying the site for the manifestation of Goddess Vana Durga Bhavani. During the monsoon, the rising waters of the Manjeera reach the feet of the Goddess — an event devotees consider highly auspicious.

text: Edupayala is regarded as one of the most powerful Shakti temples in Telangana. Goddess Vana Durga is worshipped as the divine protector who removes obstacles, grants courage, ensures prosperity, and safeguards families from negative influences. The seven sacred streams, in which pilgrims take a purifying holy bath before worship, are central to its spiritual importance. The temple is part of the Saptarishi tradition, with the seven streams named after the seven great sages.

text: The temple is especially sought for blessings of marriage, children, education, business and overall well-being, and for relief from hardships, marriage delays, health issues, financial difficulties and childlessness. Devotees believe a holy bath at the seven-stream confluence before prayers purifies body and mind. The annual Edupayala Jatara, Navaratri, Dasara and Bonalu are the most spiritually charged times to visit. The temple is one of three major Shakti temples in Telangana, alongside the others in the Jogulamba / Alampur tradition.

text: The temple is uniquely situated in the middle of the Manjeera River, where it splits into seven distinct streams. The shrine sits in a den ('Pedda Gutta Soramgam' / 'Garuda Ganga') and blends naturally with its surroundings — dense teak and bamboo forests, rocky hills, and flowing water. It features a traditional entrance (Raja Gopuram), spacious prayer halls, mandapams, and a sanctum housing the Swayambhu idol of Sri Vana Durga Bhavani. The complex includes smaller shrines to Lord Shiva, Lord Ganesha and other deities. During monsoon the seven streams flow around the temple, creating a breathtaking (and at times flood-prone) landscape. Recent infrastructure includes improved pathways, bathing ghats, queue complexes, a prasadam distribution shed, a women's dressing shed, railings, and function-hall facilities for festival crowds. A 2025 flood (Singur releases) damaged the flooring, prasadam shed, women's dressing shed, railings, surrounding sheds, CCTV cameras, electric poles and power lines (preliminary loss estimate: ₹1 crore).

Question: Which deity is worshipped in the temple?
Answer: The temple is dedicated to Goddess Sri Vana Durga Bhavani (Edupayalamma), a Swayambhu forest-form of Goddess Durga whose idol was discovered in a den called Pedda Gutta Soramgam (Garuda Ganga). Smaller shrines for Lord Shiva and Lord Ganesha are also present.

text:
Question: Why is Edupayala Temple famous?
Answer: It is famous for being located at the confluence of seven streams of the Manjeera River (the seven streams are named after the seven great sages — Jamadagni, Atri, Kasyapa, Viswamitra, Vasistha, Bharadwaja and Gautama). The annual Edupayala Jatara (around Maha Shivaratri and Magha Amavasya) is a State Festival of Telangana and one of the state's largest religious gatherings, drawing 5+ lakh devotees over three days and ~30 lakh annually.

text: Alternate names: Dharmapuri Temple Dharmapuri Narasimha Swamy Temple Sri Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy Devasthanam, Dharmapuri Dharmapuri Kshetram Pata Narasimha Swamy Temple (Old) Kottha Narasimha Swamy Temple (New) / Kotta Narasimha Swamy Temple Alternate spellings: Dharmapuri Dharmapuri Kshetram Dharmapura Dakshina Kashi Jagtial Presiding deity: Lord Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy — the man-lion incarnation (4th avatar) of Lord Vishnu — seen seated in Padmasana (Yoga Mudra) with palms on his knees, accompanied by Goddess Lakshmi; considered a rare yogic posture of the Lord Other deities: Goddess Lakshmi (consort) Lord Venkateswara Swamy (procession deity) Lord Venugopala Swamy Lord Hanuman (eight Hanuman murtis in the complex) Lord Rama Lord Krishna Lord Balarama Lord Shiva (in the sacred town, Hari-Hara Kshetra) Lord Brahma (rare 6-ft, four-faced murti — one of the few in South India) Lord Yama (Dharmaraju) at the entrance Sri Ugra Narasimha Swamy (fierce form, worshipped in the Kottha temple) Sri Yoga Narasimha Swamy Sri Saumya Narasimha Swamy Sri Prasannanjaneya Swamy (Hanuman) Sri Ramalingeshwara Swamy (Shiva) Sri Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy Temple (Dharmapuri Kshetram) in Dharmapuri, Jagtial District, Telangana, is one of the oldest and most revered Narasimha temples in South India. The presiding deity is Lord Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy, the man-lion incarnation (4th avatar) of Lord Vishnu, seen seated in Padmasana (Yoga Mudra) with Goddess Lakshmi — a posture considered rare. The temple sits on the southern bank of the Godavari River, which uniquely flows southward (Dakshina Vahini) here — a rare and highly auspicious geographical feature, earning Dharmapuri the epithet 'Dakshina Kashi' (Southern Varanasi) and 'Banaras of South India'. The town is also a 'Hari-Hara Kshetra' — a rare confluence of Vaishnava and Shaiva traditions, with both the Lakshmi Narasimha temple and several ancient Shiva temples in the sacred town. The complex includes the Pata (Old) Narasimha temple and the Kottha (New) Narasimha temple, reflecting cycles of destruction and reconstruction. It is one of the nine Nava Narasimha Kshetrams, has one of the largest settlements of Vedic Brahmins in Telangana, and is also called 'Teertharajamu' (king of pilgrimages). The next Godavari Pushkaralu will be hosted here in 2027.

metadata.temple_type: Hindu Vaishnavite Temple (Nava Narasimha Kshetram; Hari-Hara Kshetra; Dakshina Kashi)

text: section: Origin & Dynastic Patronage content: The temple has a history spanning more than a millennium. The construction period is variously cited as 850–928 AD (Trawell) and 1018 AD (per Tripadvisor reviewer citing inscriptions); the temple was originally built by the Chalukya dynasty, with later patronage from the Rashtrakutas and the Kakatiyas. Dharmapuri has long been one of the largest settlements of Vedic Brahmins in Telangana and a centre of Vedic learning, literature, and fine arts. The town is named after King Dharma Varma, who laid the foundation of the Lord's shrine. The temple is referenced in ancient texts like the Skanda Purana and Brahmanda Purana as 'Dharmapura', and is linked to legends of Lord Narasimha's meditation after slaying the demon Hiranyakashipu to protect his devotee Prahlada. It is also believed that Lord Rama visited this site and installed a sacred linga here. foundation year: c. 850–928 AD (Trawell) / 1018 AD (per inscriptions cited by Tripadvisor reviewer) founders: Chalukya dynasty (built the original temple) King Dharma Varma (laid the foundation of the Lord's shrine per local tradition; town namesake) Rashtrakutas (patronage) Kakatiyas (patronage) Panatula Narayana Deekshitulu (built the Kottha/New Narasimha temple in 1803 AD) legends: King Dharma Varma is credited with laying the foundation of the Lord's shrine; the town derives its name from him. Lord Rama is said to have visited this site and installed a sacred linga here. The temple is referenced in the Skanda Purana and Brahmanda Purana as 'Dharmapura'. The site is linked to legends of Lord Narasimha's meditation after slaying Hiranyakashipu to protect Prahlada. section: Destruction, Reconstruction & Modern Administration content: The temple was demolished by Muslim rulers during 1422–1436 AD (Rustumdil Khan, the Subedar of Hyderabad, with the support of Aurangzeb, is said to have converted it to a mosque), and was rebuilt in the 17th century, regaining its status as a major Vaishnava shrine. The Kottha (New) Narasimha Swamy Temple, also known as Sri Ugra Narasimha Swamy Temple, was built in 1803 AD by Panatula Narayana Deekshitulu and stands to the right of the Pata Narasimha temple. The temple is administered by the Telangana Endowments Department (one of 19 major temples with annual income above ₹1 crore, per the 2015 Trust Board notification). For the 2027 Godavari Pushkaralu, the Telangana government has allocated ₹50 crore for renovation, including ₹80 lakh for a new toilet complex and ₹3.1 crore for four VIP suites. The temple is a major centre for Vedic Brahmin scholars in Telangana and one of the nine Nava Narasimha Kshetrams. foundation year: 1803 AD (Kottha/New Narasimha Temple) founders: Panatula Narayana Deekshitulu (built Kottha/New Narasimha Temple in 1803 AD) legends: Temple demolished by Rustumdil Khan (Subedar of Hyderabad) with Aurangzeb's support during 1422–1436 AD; converted to a mosque. Rebuilt in the 17th century, regaining its Vaishnava identity. Kottha (New) Narasimha Temple built in 1803 AD by Panatula Narayana Deekshitulu. One of 19 major temples listed in the 2015 Telangana Trust Board notification. 2027 Godavari Pushkaralu: ₹50 crore renovation plan (₹80 lakh toilet complex, ₹3.1 crore for four VIP suites).

text: Dharmapuri is named after King Dharma Varma, who laid the foundation of the Lord's shrine. The temple's most distinctive feature is its location on the banks of the Dakshina Vahini Godavari — a stretch where the Godavari, unusually, flows southward, a direction considered highly auspicious in Hindu tradition. The town is also called 'Dakshina Kashi' (Southern Varanasi) and 'Banaras of South India', and is a 'Hari-Hara Kshetra' — a rare confluence of Vaishnava and Shaiva traditions. The temple is referenced in the Skanda Purana and Brahmanda Purana as 'Dharmapura', and is linked to legends of Lord Narasimha's meditation after slaying Hiranyakashipu. The town's dual Pata (Old) and Kottha (New) Narasimha temples reflect its passage through medieval destruction (1422–1436 AD) and reconstruction. Pilgrims traditionally take a holy dip in the Godavari before entering the temple, believing it purifies body and soul.

text: Dharmapuri is regarded as one of the holiest Narasimha temples in South India and one of the Nava Narasimha Kshetrams (nine major Narasimha shrines). It is a rare 'Hari-Hara Kshetra' — a confluence of Vaishnava and Shaiva traditions, with both the Lakshmi Narasimha temple and several ancient Shiva temples in the sacred town. It is also called 'Dakshina Kashi' (Southern Varanasi) and 'Teertharajamu' (king of pilgrimages). Lord Narasimha is worshipped here as the protector of righteousness and the destroyer of evil. The presiding deity in Padmasana (Yoga Mudra) is considered a rare form.

text: Devotees believe sincere prayers remove fear, protect families, and bring peace, prosperity and spiritual growth. The temple houses multiple forms of Lord Narasimha — peaceful and fierce manifestations (Yoga, Ugra, Saumya). The Dakshina Vahini Godavari holy bath is central to its spiritual practice, believed to purify body and soul. The temple is especially sought for protection, courage, prosperity, relief from difficulties, and for child-related and family blessings. Devotees also perform Gho Pooja for wealth and for removal of enemies.

text: The temple reflects a Dravidian style with towering gopurams, intricate carvings depicting scenes from the Ramayana and Mahabharata, and spacious mandapams including the Mukha, Garuda and Kalyana halls, leading to the sanctum via the Simha Dwaram (Lion Gate). The main deity is in a serene Padmasana (Yoga Mudra) pose flanked by Goddess Lakshmi. The complex includes three forms of Narasimha — Yoga, Ugra and Saumya — and rare sub-shrines: an idol of Yama (Dharmaraju) at the entrance, eight Hanuman murtis, and a unique 6-foot, four-faced Brahma murti (one of the few in South India). Smaller shrines house Lord Venkateswara, Sri Venugopala Swamy, Sri Prasannanjaneya Swamy, Sri Ramalingeshwara Swamy, and a Pushkarini (temple tank). The Pata (Old) and Kottha (New) Narasimha temples stand side by side. Per dharmapurikshetram.in, the temple is being prepared for the 2027 Pushkaralu with new toilet complexes and VIP suites.

text:
Question: Why is Dharmapuri Temple famous?
Answer: It is famous for being one of the nine Nava Narasimha Kshetrams, for its location on the sacred Dakshina Vahini (southward-flowing) Godavari River, for being called 'Dakshina Kashi' (Southern Varanasi) and 'Teertharajamu' (king of pilgrimages), for the rare Padmasana-form of Lord Lakshmi Narasimha, and for its status as a Hari-Hara Kshetra (Vaishnava-Shaiva harmony). The town has one of the largest settlements of Vedic Brahmins in Telangana. The next Godavari Pushkaralu is 26 June – 7 July 2027.

Question: What are the temple timings?
Answer: Per the JustDial official listing and dharmapurikshetram.in: 5:30 AM–2:30 PM and 4:00 PM–8:00 PM daily. The temple opens with Suprabhata Seva at 5:00 AM. Some other sources (Tripadvisor, Trawell, Grokipedia) give 5:00 AM–2:00 PM and 4:00 PM–8:00 PM. The 2:30 PM–4:00 PM break for darshanam is confirmed. Hours are extended during the 13-day Brahmotsavam, Narasimha Jayanthi, Vaikuntha Ekadashi and Godavari Pushkaralu.

Question: Is there an entry fee for darshan?
Answer: No. General darshan is free for all devotees. Special sevas require paid tickets: Abhishekam ₹150, Nitya Kalyanam ₹500, Sudarshana Homam ₹316, Kumkumarchana ₹100, Marriage ₹2,116, Upanayanam ₹1,516, Ganda Deepam ₹5, Swamy Aarti ₹10, plus Saswatha (perpetual) endowment poojas ranging from ₹1,116 to ₹25,116.

text:
Question: Which is the biggest festival celebrated here?
Answer: The 13-day Brahmotsavam (Phalguna Shuddha Ekadashi to Phalguna Shuddha Ashtami, Feb/Mar) is the most significant — with Kalyanotsavam, Teppotsavam (float festival on the Godavari), Dolotsavam of Sri Yoga Narasimha Swamy, and the Muvvur Swamulu chariot procession. The 2025 Brahmotsavam was 10–22 March; the 2026 one is 27 February – 11 March. Narasimha Jayanthi, Vaikuntha Ekadashi and the Godavari Pushkaralu (next: 2027) are also major celebrations.

Question: Are accommodation facilities available?
Answer: Yes. Temple guest houses and dharmashalas on-site (~₹300–₹800/day), plus private hotels and lodges in Dharmapuri town (~₹800–₹2,500/night), Jagtial (~30 km), Mancherial (~40 km), Karimnagar (~70–75 km) and Ramagundam (~65 km). For Brahmotsavam and Godavari Pushkaralu 2027, advance booking is essential; live updates are available via the dharmapurikshetram.in WhatsApp channel.

text:
Question: What is the best time to visit Dharmapuri Temple?
Answer: October to March (October–February excellent) for pleasant weather and comfortable Godavari holy baths. Best days: Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday. Most spiritually enriching: the 13-day Brahmotsavam (Feb/Mar), Narasimha Jayanthi (Vaisakha), Vaikuntha Ekadashi (December) and the Godavari Pushkaralu (next: 26 June – 7 July 2027, very crowded).

text:
Question: What is the Dakshina Vahini Godavari and why is it important?
Answer: The Godavari River, which generally flows west to east, uniquely flows from north to south (Dakshina Vahini) at Dharmapuri — a rare and highly auspicious geographical feature. Pilgrims traditionally take a holy dip in this stretch of the Godavari before entering the temple, believing it purifies body and soul. The site is called 'Dakshina Kashi' (Southern Varanasi) because of this feature. The next Godavari Pushkaralu at this site is 26 June – 7 July 2027.

text:
Question: What is special about the Padmasana-form of Lord Lakshmi Narasimha here?
Answer: Unlike the usual fierce, standing form of Lord Narasimha, the presiding deity at Dharmapuri is seen seated in Padmasana (Yoga Mudra) with his palms bending on his knees, accompanied by Goddess Lakshmi. Such a yogic posture is considered a rare form of the Lord and is one of the temple's defining features. The main deity is flanked by three forms of Narasimha — Yoga, Ugra and Saumya — symbolising peaceful, fierce and gentle aspects of the Lord.

text: Alternate names: Jamalapuram Venkateswara Swamy Temple Telangana Chinna Tirupati Khammam Chinna Tirupati Telangana Tirupati Swayambhu Venkateswara Swamy Temple, Jamalapuram Jamalapuram Balaji Temple Alternate spellings: Jamalapuram Yerrupalem Errupalem Yerupalem Swayambhoo / Swayam Vyakta Presiding deity: Lord Venkateswara ('Balaji'), a self-manifested (Swayambhu) form of Lord Vishnu, worshipped in stone (vigraha) form — a rare form like the Tirumala deity Other deities: Goddess Sri Padmavathi Ammavaru (consort) Goddess Sri Alamelu (Alivelu) Ammavaru / Alimelu Manga (consort) Lord Shiva (Sivalayam sub-shrine) Lord Ganesh (Vinayaka sub-shrine) Lord Ayyappa (Ayyappa Swamy sub-shrine) Lord Hanuman / Anjaneya Swamy (sub-shrine) Sri Venkateswara Swamy Temple at Jamalapuram, in Yerrupalem Mandal of Khammam District, Telangana, is popularly known as 'Telangana Chinna Tirupati', 'Khammam Chinna Tirupati' or 'Telangana Tirupati', reflecting devotees' belief that the deity here is comparably powerful and auspicious to Lord Venkateswara at Tirumala. The presiding deity is a self-manifested (Swayambhu) form of Lord Vishnu, worshipped as 'Balaji' in stone (vigraha) form with consorts Sri Padmavathi and Sri Alamelu (Alivelu) Ammavaru. Recognised as a Swayam Vyakta kshetra (per the official Telangana Tourism portal), it is one of the older Vaishnavite shrines in Khammam district — believed to be over 800–850 years old per the main priest (Uppala Srinivasa Sarma) and 'over 1,000 years old' per tourism sources. It was visited by the Kakatiya ruler Prataparudra on his way to Tiruvuru and renovated in the early 16th century by Vijayanagara Emperor Sri Krishnadevaraya en route to Kondapalli fort during his 'Jaitra Yatra'. A statue of Sri Krishnadevaraya stands near the Pongali Mandapam (installed c. 2010 to mark the 500th anniversary of his coronation). The temple draws large crowds, especially on Saturdays and during Brahmotsavam, Vaikunta Ekadasi and Dwadasi.

text: section: Historical Background & Royal Patronage content: The temple is one of the older Vaishnavite shrines in Khammam district. Per the main priest Uppala Srinivasa Sarma (quoted in 2017 press reports), it is believed to be more than 800–850 years old; some tourism sources describe it as 'over 1,000 years old' — both estimates are widely repeated. The temple is said to have been visited by the Kakatiya ruler Prataparudra on his way to Tiruvuru, and later renovated by the Vijayanagara Emperor Sri Krishnadevaraya, who offered prayers here en route to Kondapalli fort during his military campaign known as the 'Jaitra Yatra'. The temple is also described as having flourished as a gurukulam (seat of learning) under the sage Jabali. Around 2010, a statue of Sri Krishnadevaraya was installed near the Pongali Mandapam as part of celebrations marking the 500th anniversary of his coronation. Located in a pollution-free area surrounded by lush green hills and the Pedda Cheruvu (temple tank), the temple is recognised as a Swayam Vyakta kshetra on the official Telangana Tourism portal. foundation year: 800–1,000+ years (variously reported); renovated early 16th century by Sri Krishnadevaraya (1509–1529 CE) founders: Sage Jabali Maharshi (legendary, per temple tradition) Kakatiya ruler Prataparudra (historical visitor/patron) Vijayanagara Emperor Sri Krishnadevaraya (renovator, early 16th c.) Main priest (current): Uppala Srinivasa Sarma (per 2017 press) legends: Sage Jabali performed penance at Suchi Gutta (Soochi Giri) and was blessed with a vision of Lord Vishnu, who manifested as an icon. The temple is said to have been visited by Kakatiya ruler Prataparudra en route to Tiruvuru. Renovated by Vijayanagara Emperor Sri Krishnadevaraya en route to Kondapalli fort during his 'Jaitra Yatra' (early 16th c.). A statue of Sri Krishnadevaraya was installed near the Pongali Mandapam c. 2010 (500th coronation anniversary celebrations). section: Founding Legends (two irreconcilable versions) content: Two versions of the temple's founding legend are repeated across sources; both are presented as they could not be reconciled into a single canonical account from an official source. (1) Jabali Maharshi legend: the sage performed penance at a hillock here called Suchi Gutta (Soochi Giri), after which he was blessed with a vision of Lord Vishnu, who manifested as an icon at the spot. (2) Uppala Yagnanarayana Sharma / Akku Bhatlu legend: a devotee named Uppala Yagnanarayana Sharma paused here during a Kashi pilgrimage and settled; he felt a mysterious pull, and Lord Venkateswara came as a child to play with cattlemen every day. If anyone asked the child's name and place, he would answer 'your signature is my name, your location is my place'. Yagnanarayana Sharma eventually recognised the child and climbed to the top of the hill to worship him, where he discovered the Lord Venkateswara icon and inscriptions on the stone. A related version of the legend: his sixth descendant Uppala Akku Bhatlu — unable to climb the hill — prayed for guidance, and Lord Venkateswara instructed him to descend without looking back so the Lord could follow; Akku Bhatlu turned on hearing a loud sound, at which point the deity manifested (Swayambhu) at that spot. legends: Jabali Maharshi performed penance at Suchi Gutta and was granted a vision of Lord Vishnu, who manifested as an icon. Uppala Yagnanarayana Sharma paused here during a Kashi pilgrimage, felt a mysterious pull, and settled; Lord Venkateswara came as a child to play with cattlemen, eventually revealing himself. Uppala Akku Bhatlu, a later descendant, was instructed by the Lord to descend the hill without looking back; on turning at a loud sound, the deity self-manifested (Swayambhu) at that spot.

text: Per temple lore (recorded only in tourism/blog sources), sage Jabali performed penance at the Suchi Gutta (Soochi Giri) hillock here and was blessed with a vision of Lord Vishnu, who manifested as a Swayambhu icon. An alternate legend holds that the devotee Uppala Yagnanarayana Sharma paused here during a Kashi pilgrimage, felt a mysterious pull, and settled; Lord Venkateswara came as a child to play with cattlemen every day, eventually revealing himself. A related version says his descendant Uppala Akku Bhatlu was instructed by Lord Venkateswara to descend the hill without looking back; on turning at a loud sound, the deity self-manifested (Swayambhu) at that spot. The temple is thus a Swayambhu / Swayam Vyakta kshetra, likened to Tirumala as 'Telangana Chinna Tirupati'.

text: Devotees believe darshan and puja here lead to the fulfilment of wishes, akin to beliefs about the Tirumala Venkateswara temple. Saturdays are especially popular for worship (per the official Telangana Tourism portal). Passing through the temple's Vaikunta Dwaram on Vaikunta Ekadasi / Dwadasi is believed to grant spiritual passage to Vaikunta, Lord Vishnu's abode. The temple's serene, pollution-free, green-hilled setting is cited as conducive to peaceful meditation.

text: The temple features a five-tier Gopuram (entrance tower) with a Dhwaja Stambham (flag post) placed within it, and a Pongali Mandapam. The temple tank is known locally as Pedda Cheruvu. The complex follows South Indian temple architectural style and includes sub-shrines dedicated to Sri Padmavathi Ammavaru, Sri Alamelu (Alivelu / Alimelu Manga) Ammavaru, Lord Shiva (Sivalayam), Lord Ganesh, Lord Ayyappa, and Lord Hanuman / Anjaneya Swamy. A statue of Emperor Sri Krishnadevaraya was installed near the Pongali Mandapam around 2010 as part of the 500th coronation anniversary celebrations. The temple is located amidst pleasant weather surrounded by lush green hills on the Telangana-AP border, which contributes to the calm atmosphere of the complex.

text:
Question: Why is it called 'Telangana Chinna Tirupati'?
Answer: Because devotees consider the deity here comparably powerful and auspicious to Lord Venkateswara at Tirumala (Tirupati), and the temple shares the Swayambhu Venkateswara worship tradition. The temple is officially recognised as a Swayam Vyakta kshetra by the Telangana Tourism portal.

text:
Question: How old is the temple?
Answer: Estimates vary: the main priest Uppala Srinivasa Sarma (cited in 2017) described it as more than 800–850 years old, while some tourism sources say 'over 1,000 years old'. The structure was significantly renovated in the early 16th century under Vijayanagara Emperor Sri Krishnadevaraya.

text:
Question: How do I get to Jamalapuram?
Answer: By road via bus from Khammam (~75–86 km) or Vijayawada (~52–56 km, the most geographically plausible figure — Yerrupalem is on the Telangana-AP border along NH65). By rail to Errupalem (Yerrupalem) station (~6–7.5 km); the Krishna Express and Golconda Express pass through. By air via Gannavaram Airport, Vijayawada (~52–73 km). Hyderabad is ~260 km away.

Question: What is the legend of Suchi Gutta and sage Jabali?
Answer: Per temple tradition, sage Jabali performed penance at the Suchi Gutta (Soochi Giri) hillock at the temple site and was blessed with a vision of Lord Vishnu, who manifested as an icon. The hillock is still associated with the temple and is visited by devotees as part of the pilgrimage.

text: Alternate names: Manyamkonda Temple Pedala Tirupati Poor Man's Tirupati Palamoor Tirupati Telangana Tirupati Sri Lakshmi Venkateshwara Swamy Temple, Manyamkonda Alternate spellings: Manyamkonda Mannemkonda Munulakonda Pedala Tirupati Palamoor Tirupati Koilkonda Mandal Oblaipalle Presiding deity: Lord Lakshmi Venkateswara Swamy — a Swayambhu (self-manifested) stone idol ('Chekkani Shilpam') in a natural cave ('Kattani gudi') on Manyamkonda Hill; an incarnation of Lord Vishnu, with consorts Sridevi (Lakshmi) and Bhudevi Other deities: Goddess Lakshmi (Sridevi, consort) Goddess Bhudevi (consort) Lord Hanuman Lord Garuda Lord Ganesha Alwars and Vaishnavite saints Lord Shiva (in a separate cave temple near the main shrine) Alivelu Manga Temple (Padmavati-like, at the starting point of the Ghat road) Manyamkonda Lakshmi Venkateswara Swamy Temple is one of the most revered hill temples in Telangana, located near Manyamkonda village (also called Oblaipalle) in Koilkonda Mandal, Mahabubnagar district — about 5 km from Devarakadra town on NH 167 towards Raichur, and ~18 km from Mahabubnagar. Dedicated to a Swayambhu (self-manifested) stone idol ('Chekkani Shilpam') of Lord Lakshmi Venkateswara Swamy (Vishnu) in a natural cave ('Kattani gudi'), with consorts Sridevi and Bhudevi, it is popularly known as 'Pedala Tirupati' (Poor Man's Tirupati) or 'Palamoor Tirupati', because devotees believe worshipping here bestows blessings similar to those at Tirumala. The hill was earlier known as 'Munulakonda' (after Munula = Saint + Konda = Hill) and was the meditation place of saints like Narasimha Yogi, Kasirayalu, Ettepu Ramayogi, Veerappaiah and Yanumaddhasu; it was later renamed Manyamkonda. The temple — believed to be ~500 years old and the first temple in Telangana to have ropeway access — attracts thousands of pilgrims, especially during its annual Brahmotsavam (Jaathara, Jan/Feb), Vaikunta Ekadasi and other major festivals.

text: section: Historical Background & Saints content: The temple's history dates back several centuries (believed to be ~500 years old). The hill was earlier known as 'Munulakonda' (from Munula = Saint + Konda = Hill in Telugu), because it was the meditation place of several saints and spiritual gurus, including Narasimha Yogi, Kasirayalu, Ettepu Ramayogi, Veerappaiah and Yanumaddhasu. Over time, the hill came to be called Manyamkonda. Per local belief, Lord Venkateswara manifested himself on Manyamkonda Hill to bless devotees who were unable to undertake the arduous Tirumala pilgrimage — the origin of the temple's popular name 'Pedala Tirupati' (Poor Man's Tirupati) / 'Palamoor Tirupati'. The presiding deity is a Swayambhu (self-manifested) stone idol ('Chekkani Shilpam') in a natural cave ('Kattani gudi'), with consorts Sridevi (Lakshmi) and Bhudevi. A separate Shiva temple exists in the caves near the main shrine, and an Alivelu Manga Temple (Padmavati-like) stands at the starting point of the Ghat road. The temple was the first in Telangana to have ropeway access, and it has been renovated periodically by devotees and the Telangana Endowments Department to preserve its spiritual and cultural heritage. foundation year: ~500 years old (per temple-timings.blogspot.com) legends: Lord Venkateswara manifested himself on Manyamkonda Hill to bless devotees unable to undertake the Tirumala pilgrimage. The hill was the meditation place of saints Narasimha Yogi, Kasirayalu, Ettepu Ramayogi, Veerappaiah and Yanumaddhasu. Originally called 'Munulakonda' (Saint Hill), later renamed Manyamkonda. The temple is the first in Telangana to have ropeway access (per Wikipedia).

text: The hill was originally known as 'Munulakonda' — 'Munula' (saint) + 'Konda' (hill) in Telugu — because of the many saints who meditated there, including Narasimha Yogi, Kasirayalu, Ettepu Ramayogi, Veerappaiah and Yanumaddhasu. Per local tradition, Lord Venkateswara later manifested himself on the hilltop as a Swayambhu stone idol ('Chekkani Shilpam') in a natural cave ('Kattani gudi') to bless devotees who could not undertake the arduous pilgrimage to Tirumala. This gave the temple its popular name 'Pedala Tirupati' (Poor Man's Tirupati) / 'Palamoor Tirupati', signifying that the blessings of Tirumala's Venkateswara are accessible to all at Manyamkonda. The temple also has a separate Shiva temple in the caves nearby, and a Tavvani Koneru (naturally formed lake).

metadata.category: Vaishnavite / Venkateswara Temple (Swayambhu hill shrine; 'Pedala Tirupati' / 'Palamoor Tirupati')

text: Manyamkonda is considered one of the most sacred Vaishnavite shrines in Telangana. It is known as 'Pedala Tirupati' (Poor Man's Tirupati) / 'Palamoor Tirupati' / 'Telangana Tirupati' because devotees believe worshipping here bestows blessings similar to those received at Tirumala, making it an accessible pilgrimage destination for all — particularly those for whom the Tirumala pilgrimage is difficult. The Swayambhu form of the deity, the natural cave setting, and the ropeway access reinforce its status as a 'miracle' hill shrine.

text: Devotees believe worshipping Lord Venkateswara here removes obstacles, fulfils wishes, and brings prosperity, health and spiritual well-being. Many visit before important events such as marriages, examinations and new business ventures. The ropeway access to the hilltop shrine is itself considered a unique blessing, and the cave temple (Kattani gudi) is believed to be a powerful site for meditation, in the tradition of the saints who preceded the temple.

text: The temple is built in traditional South Indian temple architecture atop a scenic hill. The entrance is marked by a beautifully decorated Rajagopuram with images of gods and goddesses carved on it. The presiding deity is a Swayambhu stone idol in the natural cave ('Kattani gudi'); there is also a Koneru (sacred pond) within the complex. The complex includes a spacious mandapam, shrines for Goddess Lakshmi, Lord Hanuman, Lord Garuda, Lord Ganesha and the Alwars / Vaishnavite saints. The complex also has a separate Lord Shiva temple in the caves, and an Alivelu Manga Temple at the base of the hill (at the starting point of the Ghat road). A ropeway provides access to the hilltop — the first in Telangana.

text:
Question: Why is Manyamkonda Temple called Pedala Tirupati?
Answer: Because devotees believe worshipping Lord Venkateswara here offers blessings similar to those of Tirumala, making it an accessible pilgrimage destination — hence 'Pedala Tirupati' (Poor Man's Tirupati). It is also called 'Palamoor Tirupati' and 'Telangana Tirupati'.

text:
Question: Which deity is worshipped here?
Answer: The presiding deity is Lord Lakshmi Venkateswara Swamy, a Swayambhu (self-manifested) stone idol ('Chekkani Shilpam') in a natural cave ('Kattani gudi') on Manyamkonda Hill, with consorts Goddess Sridevi (Lakshmi) and Goddess Bhudevi. There are also shrines to Lord Hanuman, Lord Garuda, Lord Ganesha, the Alwars / Vaishnavite saints, and a separate Lord Shiva temple in the caves.

text:
Question: What is unique about this temple?
Answer: Three things make it unique: (1) It is the first temple in Telangana to have ropeway access; (2) the presiding deity is a Swayambhu stone idol in a natural cave (Kattani gudi) on a hill, with a Tavvani Koneru (naturally formed lake); (3) it sits on Munulakonda / Manyamkonda Hill, the meditation place of saints Narasimha Yogi, Kasirayalu, Ettepu Ramayogi, Veerappaiah and Yanumaddhasu.

text:
Question: How can I reach the temple?
Answer: By road from Mahabubnagar (~18 km on NH 167) or Hyderabad (~110 km). Buses run from Hyderabad, Mahabubnagar and Raichur to Manyamkonda village; autos are available from the village to the Ghat road. Two routes to the hilltop: Ghat road (for vehicles) and traditional stone steps (trekking). A ropeway provides easy access — the first ropeway-accessed temple in Telangana. The nearest railway station is Mahabubnagar, and the nearest airport is Hyderabad (~110 km).

text: Alternate names: Beechupally Hanuman Temple Sri Anjaneya Swamy Temple, Beechupally Beechupally Anjaneya Swamy Temple Beechupally Brahmana Satram (associated) Dakshina Kashi Gateway to Srisailam Beechupalli Sri Anjaneya Swamy Devalayam Alternate spellings: Beechupally Bichupally Beechupalli Beechpally Itikyala Itikyal Erravalli Chowrasta Presiding deity: Lord Hanuman (Sri Abhaya Anjaneya Swamy / 'Sankata Mochana Anjaneya' — remover of troubles), worshipped in a standing idol covered with a silver Kavach; one of the few Hanuman idols believed to bear the 'Sanku Chakra' (conch and discus) marks. The idol is said to have been installed by Sri Vyasaraya (Vyasaraja), the royal guru of Vijayanagara Emperor Sri Krishna Devaraya, ~200 years ago. Other deities: Lord Rama (large temple dedicated to Sri Rama, constructed in 1992 a little away from the bank) Lord Shiva (a Siva Linga on the river bank that gets wetted by the Krishna's waters during the peak monsoon) Several other deities within the Sri Rama complex (1992) The Sri Abhaya Anjaneya Swamy Temple (Beechupally Hanuman Temple) is one of the most cherished Hanuman shrines in Telangana, nestled along the banks of the River Krishna, on NH-44 (formerly NH-7), in Beechupally village of Itikyala Mandal, Jogulamba Gadwal district — close to the Telangana–Karnataka border. Often called Dakshina Kashi and regarded as the 'Gateway to Srisailam', it draws thousands of devotees each year — particularly Srisailam padayatris and those performing asthi visarjan (Astikalu nimajjan) at the adjacent Pushkar Ghat. Per temple tradition, the idol was installed ~200 years ago by Sri Vyasaraya (Vyasaraja), the royal guru of Vijayanagara Emperor Sri Krishna Devaraya; a young tribal boy named 'Beechupally' (after whom the village is named) made daily offerings, and Lord Hanuman is locally known as 'Beechupally Rayudu'. The temple is revered as a Hanuman Siddha Kshetram where devotees seek strength, courage, freedom from fear, success in exams/jobs/court cases, and remedies for Shani and Kuja dosha. The idol, covered with a silver Kavach, is one of the few said to bear the 'Sanku Chakra' marks. A 1992-constructed Sri Rama temple stands nearby, and two islands (Gurram Gadda and Nizam Konda) dot the Krishna opposite the shrine.

text: section: Origin & Vijayanagara Patronage content: The temple is ~200 years old (per Hyderabad Zone, xploringdestinations). Per temple tradition, the idol of Lord Hanuman was installed by Sri Vyasaraya (Vyasaraja), the illustrious royal guru (rajaguru) of the Vijayanagara Emperor Sri Krishna Devaraya. After installing the idol, Vyasaraya left the area. That night, Lord Hanuman appeared in his dream and revealed that a young tribal boy named 'Beechupally' had been making daily prayers to the idol — and so the village came to be called Beechupally, and the Lord is locally known as 'Beechupally Rayudu'. Originally, only the Valmiki community served as priests; later, Madhwa Brahmins (with the support of the Gadwal Rulers) were also allowed to perform rituals. The Gadwal Rulers conducted the annual religious chariot festival and supported the temple; this patronage continued as a tradition. In 1950, a road bridge across the Krishna was constructed (with a later NH-7 / now NH-44 highway passing through the village), opening up trade and transit from Rayalaseema to central India. In 1992, a large Sri Rama temple was constructed a little away from the river bank, housing several other deities. The temple sits on the banks of the Krishna River, ~30 km downstream of the Jurala Hydro Electric Project, with two islands (Gurram Gadda, Nizam Konda) opposite the shrine. foundation year: ~200 years old (per multiple sources); idol installed by Sri Vyasaraya (Vyasaraja), the royal guru of Vijayanagara Emperor Sri Krishna Devaraya founders: Sri Vyasaraya (Vyasaraja) — Vijayanagara royal guru, installed the idol Gadwal Rulers — historical patrons (annual chariot festival, support for rituals) Madhwa Brahmins — extended priestly tradition (along with original Valmiki community) Beechupally Brahmana Nitya Annadana Trust (modern) — provides annadana for pilgrims legends: Sri Vyasaraya (Vyasaraja), the royal guru of Emperor Sri Krishna Devaraya, installed the idol of Lord Hanuman here. After installing, Vyasaraya left; that night, Lord Hanuman appeared in his dream and told him that a young tribal boy named 'Beechupally' had been making daily prayers to the idol — the village is named after this boy. Per Ramayana tradition, Lord Hanuman paused at Beechupally while carrying the Sanjeevani mountain to Lanka; prayers offered here are believed to go straight to Lord Rama through Hanuman. The Hanuman idol is one of the few said to bear the 'Sanku Chakra' (conch and discus) marks, though the marks are covered by the silver Kavach. Originally only the Valmiki community served as priests; later Madhwa Brahmins (with Gadwal Ruler support) were also allowed to perform rituals. The Krishna River at this stretch gets the Shiva Linga on the bank wet during peak monsoon — a natural devotional phenomenon. Every 12 years, the Krishna Pushkaralu turn the river's waters into 'supernatural-power' pilgrimage sites; the Telangana State government has built permanent bathing ghats for the event.

After installing, Vyasaraya left the area. That night, Lord Hanuman appeared in his dream and revealed that a young tribal boy named 'Beechupally' had been making daily prayers to the idol — and so the village came to be called Beechupally, and the Lord is locally known as 'Beechupally Rayudu'. The Gadwal Rulers conducted the annual religious chariot festival and supported the temple. The riverside location also made it a natural and revered halt for pilgrims (including padayatra groups) travelling to the Srisailam Mallikarjuna Jyotirlinga — hence its epithet 'Gateway to Srisailam' / 'Dakshina Kashi'.

text: Beechupally is a Hanuman Siddha Kshetram, popularly called Dakshina Kashi, and is regarded as the 'Gateway to Srisailam'. It is a significant stop for devotees on the way to the Srisailam Mallikarjuna Jyotirlinga; many believe seeking Hanuman's blessings here before continuing to Srisailam makes the journey safer and obstacle-free. Padayatra (foot pilgrimage) groups traditionally rest and pray here, and the Pushkar Ghat is a major site for asthi visarjan (Astikalu nimajjan) for families from Telangana, Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka.

The deity is revered as 'Sankata Mochana Anjaneya' — the remover of troubles. The temple is sought for strength and courage, freedom from fear, success in exams/jobs/court cases, and relief from planetary doshas (particularly Shani and Kuja dosha). text: The temple is built in the South Indian architectural style and is ~200 years old. The Garbhagriha (sanctum) houses a standing idol of Lord Hanuman covered with a silver Kavach, with the deity facing east and the temple facing south. Open mandapams invite the refreshing river breeze and natural light. A Siva Linga on the river bank gets wetted by the Krishna's waters during the peak monsoon. A 1992-constructed large Sri Rama temple stands a little away from the bank, with several other deities within the complex. The temple is on the banks of the Krishna River, ~30 km downstream of the Jurala Hydro Electric Project, on NH-44. The Pushkar Ghat adjacent to the temple has permanent bathing ghats built by the Telangana State government for Krishna Pushkaralu and asthi visarjan.

text:
Question: Why is Beechupally Hanuman Temple famous?
Answer: It is renowned for its powerful idol of Lord Hanuman ('Sankata Mochana Anjaneya', remover of troubles) installed ~200 years ago by Sri Vyasaraya (Vyasaraja), the royal guru of Vijayanagara Emperor Sri Krishna Devaraya; the silver-Kavach-covered idol is one of the few said to bear the unique 'Sanku Chakra' marks. It is a Hanuman Siddha Kshetram, popularly called Dakshina Kashi and the 'Gateway to Srisailam', and a key stop for Srisailam padayatris and asthi visarjan (Astikalu nimajjan) at the adjacent Pushkar Ghat.

Question: Who installed the Hanuman idol?
Answer: Per temple tradition, Sri Vyasaraya (Vyasaraja) — the illustrious royal guru (rajaguru) of Vijayanagara Emperor Sri Krishna Devaraya — installed the idol of Lord Hanuman here ~200 years ago. After installing, Vyasaraya left; that night, Lord Hanuman appeared in his dream and told him that a young tribal boy named 'Beechupally' had been making daily prayers to the idol — and the village came to be called Beechupally, with the Lord locally known as 'Beechupally Rayudu'.

text: Alternate names: Sammakka Saralamma Jatara Medaram Jathara Sammakka Sarakka Jatara Medaram Maha Jathara Medaram Tribal Jathara Asia's largest tribal religious congregation Alternate spellings: Medaram Sammakka Sarakka Sammakka Saralamma Saralamma Sarakka Medaram Jathara Presiding deity: Goddess Sammakka (Sammakka Ammavaru) and her daughter Goddess Saralamma (Sarakka / Saralamma Ammavaru) — the tribal mother-daughter duo revered as forest goddesses (Devathas). Goddess Sammakka is the primary presiding deity; her idol is at Chilakala Gutta in the form of a 'Kumkuma Bharina' (a vermilion-form deity). Other deities: Goddess Saralamma (Sarakka) — daughter of Sammakka, installed at Kannepally village Pagididda Raju — Sammakka's husband and a feudatory tribal chief of the Kakatiyas Govindaraju (Govinda Raju) — associated deity taken back to the forest after the Jathara Jampanna — Sammakka's son, the tribal warrior who died fighting the Kakatiyan Army at Jampanna Vagu Sri Sammakka Saralamma Temple at Medaram, in the heart of the Eturnagaram Wildlife Sanctuary (Dandakaranya forest belt), Tadvai Mandal, Mulugu District, Telangana, is the site of Asia's largest tribal religious congregation — the Sammakka Saralamma Jatara (Medaram Jathara), held biennially in honour of the tribal mother-daughter duo Sammakka and Saralamma. Declared a State Festival in 1998, the Jathara draws 1.5–3 crore devotees over four days (next: 28–31 January 2028, with 2026 having just concluded), making it the largest gathering in India after the Kumbh Mela. The rituals are performed entirely by Koya tribe priests in accordance with their customs (no Vedic or Brahmanic influence). Devotees offer 'Bangaram' (jaggery, equal to their weight in some traditions), 'Odi Biyyam' (sacred rice) and take a holy dip in the red waters of Jampanna Vagu (named after the tribal warrior Jampanna, who died fighting the Kakatiyan Army in that stream). The temple complex is administered by a non-hereditary chairman board, with MLA Santosh Chakravarthy having served as the first chairman (appointed 27 April 1968). The Telangana government reconstructed the altars of the deities (Sammakka, Saralamma, Govindaraju, Pagididda Raju) at a cost of ~₹101 crore ahead of the 2026 Jathara, with additional ₹150 crore in development works.

text: section: 13th-century Origin & the Kakatiya Revolt content: Per tribal tradition, the goddess Sammakka and her daughter Saralamma were tribal leaders who lived in the 12th–13th centuries and led a revolt against the Kakatiya rulers' unjust tax on the tribal populace during a prolonged drought. Sammakka was married to Pagididda Raju, a feudatory tribal chief of the Kakatiyas (who ruled the country of Andhra from Warangal City between 1000 AD and 1380 AD). She was blessed with 2 daughters and 1 son: Sarakka, Nagulamma and Jampanna respectively. Jampanna was a tribal warrior who died fighting the Kakatiyan Army at a stream (now named Jampanna Vagu after him; the water is reportedly red in colour — scientifically attributed to the soil composition, but tribally believed to be marked with Jampanna's blood). Per tribal legend, it was Sammakka's curse which caused the gradual decline and death of the Kakatiya rule. The Jathara commemorates their sacrifice and is the largest repeating tribal religious congregation in the world. foundation year: 13th century (per tribal tradition; legend dates back ~700 years) legends: Sammakka was born ~6–7 centuries ago (13th century), when tribal leaders on a hunt found a newborn girl emitting enormous light playing amidst tigers; the head of the tribe adopted and raised her as a chieftain. Sammakka married Pagididda Raju, a feudatory tribal chief of the Kakatiyas, and had 2 daughters (Sarakka/Saralamma, Nagulamma) and 1 son (Jampanna). Sammakka led a tribal revolt against the unjust Kakatiya tax on tribals during a drought. Her son Jampanna died fighting the Kakatiyan Army at a stream (now Jampanna Vagu); the water is still reddish — tribally believed to be marked with his blood. Sammakka's curse is said to have caused the gradual decline and death of the Kakatiya rule. Saralamma is installed in a temple at Kannepally, a small village near Medaram; Sammakka is at Chilakala Gutta in the form of a 'Kumkuma Bharina' (vermilion form). The tribal goddesses are believed to 'visit' their devotees during the Jathara period; after 4 days, the goddesses return to the forest (Vana Pravesham). section: Modern Era: 1946, 1955, 1998, 2026 content: Until 1955, only about 2,000 people visited Medaram, of whom the majority (1,500) belonged to the Koya tribe. In 1946, the Jatara was held with greater fervour and attendance than ever before under the supervision of Subedar Amir Ali Khan, who instituted multiple water stations, first-aid posts, mobile medical units, traffic regulation, sanitation, and crowd management — widely cited as a precedent-setting public welfare effort. Until 1998, the only way to reach Medaram was by bullock cart; in that year, the state government declared the 1,000-year-old festival as official (a State Festival) and laid down a motorable road. MLA Santosh Chakravarthy was appointed as the first chairman of the Sammakka Sarakka Temple on 27 April 1968. In 2008, ~8 million people attended; today attendance is ~10 million+ per cycle. The 2012 Jathara attracted ~1 crore people. The 2026 Jathara (28–31 January 2026) was the largest yet: an estimated 80 lakh devotees on the first two days alone, with the full 4-day total estimated at nearly 3 crore; the Telangana government deployed 21 government departments, 42,027 personnel, ~9,000 police officers, hundreds of CCTV cameras and 2 drone cameras, and ~500 NSS volunteers from Kakatiya University, Warangal. The government reconstructed the altars of Sammakka, Saralamma, Govindaraju and Pagididda Raju at a cost of ~₹101 crore, with additional ₹150 crore in development works (parking, water stations, sanitation, medical camps, temporary bridges). The 2026 Jathara concluded at 7:55 PM on 31 January 2026 with Vana Pravesham (return to the forest). foundation year: Recognized as State Festival in 1998; motorable road laid in 1998; altar reconstruction completed for 2026 founders: Koya tribe (traditional custodians and priests) Subedar Amir Ali Khan (1946 — pioneer of modern public welfare arrangements) MLA Santosh Chakravarthy (first chairman of the Sammakka Sarakka Temple board, appointed 27 April 1968) Government of Telangana (since 1998 — State Festival status, infrastructure) legends: 1946: Subedar Amir Ali Khan's stewardship of the Jathara set a precedent for public welfare (water stations, medical camps, traffic, sanitation). 1998: State Festival declared; motorable road laid; the festival took a modern shape. 1968: MLA Santosh Chakravarthy appointed first chairman of the Sammakka Sarakka Temple board. 2008: ~8 million attendees; 2012: ~1 crore attendees. 2026: ~80 lakh on days 1–2, nearly 3 crore total; ₹101 crore altar reconstruction + ₹150 crore development works; 21 government departments, 42,000+ personnel, ~9,000 police, 2 drone cameras, ~500 NSS volunteers; concluded at 7:55 PM on 31 Jan 2026.

text: Per tribal tradition, goddess Sammakka was born in the 13th century, found as a newborn emitting enormous light amid tigers, and was adopted by the head of the Koya tribe. She married Pagididda Raju, a feudatory tribal chief of the Kakatiyas, and had 2 daughters (Sarakka/Saralamma and Nagulamma) and 1 son (Jampanna). When the Kakatiya rulers imposed an unjust tax on the tribals during a prolonged drought, Sammakka and her daughter Saralamma led a tribal revolt. Jampanna, Sammakka's son and a tribal warrior, died fighting the Kakatiyan Army at a stream (now Jampanna Vagu after him; the water is still reddish — tribally believed to be marked with his blood). Sammakka's curse is said to have caused the gradual decline and death of the Kakatiya rule. The forest goddesses are believed to 'visit' their devotees during the biennial Jathara, after which they return to the forest (Vana Pravesham) — the focal point of the four-day festival. The rituals are entirely performed by Koya tribe priests in accordance with their customs, with no Vedic or Brahmanic influence.

text: Sammakka Saralamma Temple at Medaram is the site of Asia's largest tribal religious congregation and a State Festival of Telangana (since 1998). It is the largest gathering in India after the Kumbh Mela. The temple is a non-Vedic, non-Brahmanic shrine entirely administered by Koya tribe priests in accordance with their customs. It is a major centre for tribal religious identity, drawing 1.5–3 crore devotees from Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka and Jharkhand. Devotees offer Bangaram (jaggery), Odi Biyyam (sacred rice), turmeric, vermilion, rice and cloth; women offer sarees; and pilgrims take a holy dip in the red waters of Jampanna Vagu. The temple is revered as a symbol of tribal resistance, women's leadership (Sammakka as a female warrior-chieftain) and forest-deity devotion. The 2026 Jathara was inaugurated by the Telangana Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy on 19 January 2026 (reconstructed shrine inauguration).

text: Devotees believe Sammakka and Saralamma are forest goddesses (Devathas) who 'visit' their devotees during the Jathara period and return to the forest after four days (Vana Pravesham). The rituals performed at the gaddelu (sacred altar) are believed to bestow protection, fulfilment of vows (Mokubadulu), and ancestral blessings. Devotees come seeking solutions to personal and family problems, court cases, marital issues, child-related concerns, and protection of tribal lands and forests. The red water of Jampanna Vagu is believed to remind tribals of the sacrifice of their gods and to induce courage in their souls. The festival is a major assertion of tribal cultural identity and continuity, and the journey to Medaram itself is considered a sacred pilgrimage.

text: The Sammakka Saralamma Temple at Medaram has a distinct tribal-Shaivite architecture, blending folk-tribal elements with simple South Indian temple features. The gaddelu (sacred altar) is the focal point of the four-day Jathara, where the deities are ceremonially installed. Saralamma is installed in a temple at Kannepally (a small village near Medaram), and Sammakka is at Chilakala Gutta in the form of a 'Kumkuma Bharina' (a vermilion-form deity — i.e. the goddess is represented by a mound of vermilion rather than a stone or metal idol). The complex is in the heart of the Eturnagaram Wildlife Sanctuary (Dandakaranya forest belt). The Telangana government reconstructed the altars of the deities (Sammakka, Saralamma, Govindaraju, Pagididda Raju) at a cost of ~₹101 crore ahead of the 2026 Jathara. The Jampanna Vagu (a tributary of the Godavari) flows through the forest region, with a bridge constructed on top of it (Jampanna Vagu bridge). The complex includes Forest Tents (100 tents set up by the Forest Department; up to 5 persons per tent; 24-hour/12-hour rentals), Kalyana Katta, Ballon No. 5, and 21 government department-managed facilities.

For off-season visitors, October to February is the most pleasant weather window, though the temple is in the deep Eturnagaram Wildlife Sanctuary and may be closed to non-tribal visitors outside the Jathara. Avoid peak days (Day 3 — Friday) if you dislike crowds (up to 40 lakh on the busiest day per 2026 arrangements). Pilgrims are advised to arrive early in the morning, carry water, wear light traditional clothing, and be prepared for significant walking and queueing.

text: road: Medaram is ~90 km from Warangal city. Until 1998, the only way to reach Medaram was by bullock cart; in 1998, the state government laid down a motorable road. For the 2026 Jathara, TSRTC ran nearly 4,000 buses daily to move around 21 lakh people, with 30 bus points to Medaram. Special buses run from all areas of Telangana. From Hyderabad, the route is via Warangal; from Warangal, local buses and special Jathara buses. Buses also connect from Bhupalpally, Kothagudem, Mancherial, Karimnagar, and the surrounding districts. Massive parking areas are set up for the 4-day festival. The official website lists TGSRTC fares (e.g., Godavarikhani 175 km ₹400; Peddapalli 185 km ₹420; Manthani 150 km ₹350; B-Incline 175 km ₹400). rail: Nearest major railway station is Warangal (~90 km). Kazipet Junction is also a major railhead (~95 km). The Hyderabad + Greater Hyderabad regions together accounted for more than 5.18 lakh bus passengers during the 2026 Jathara, while Warangal zones and Karimnagar region also contributed significantly. air: Nearest airport is Rajiv Gandhi International Airport, Hyderabad (~300 km, 5–6 hours by road). distances: Hyderabad: ~300 km (~5–6 hours by road) Warangal: ~90 km (the closest major city, base for many pilgrims) Bhupalpally (Jayashankar Bhupalpally): ~30 km Kothagudem: ~120 km Mancherial: ~150 km Karimnagar: ~150 km Eturnagaram Wildlife Sanctuary: at the temple site Ramappa Temple: ~50 km Laknavaram Lake: ~35 km nearest railway station: Warangal Railway Station (~90 km) nearest bus station: Medaram village bus stop (on the 1998 motorable road; 30+ TSRTC bus points to Medaram during the Jathara) nearest airport: Rajiv Gandhi International Airport, Hyderabad (~300 km)

text:
Question: What is the Sammakka Saralamma Jatara?
Answer: It is a biennial tribal religious festival held in honour of the tribal mother-daughter goddesses Sammakka and Saralamma at Medaram village in Tadvai Mandal, Mulugu District, Telangana. It is recognised as Asia's largest tribal religious congregation, drawing 1.5 to 3 crore devotees over 4 days — the largest gathering in India after the Kumbh Mela. Declared a State Festival in 1998, it is performed entirely by Koya tribe priests in accordance with their customs (no Vedic or Brahmanic influence). The 2026 cycle was 28–31 January 2026; the next is expected January 2028.

Question: Where is the Sammakka Saralamma Temple located?
Answer: In Medaram village, Tadvai Mandal, Mulugu District, Telangana – 506344, India. The temple is in the heart of the Eturnagaram Wildlife Sanctuary (Dandakaranya forest belt), ~90 km from Warangal city and ~300 km from Hyderabad. The gaddelu (sacred altar) is the focal point of the Jathara; the Saralamma temple is in nearby Kannepally; Sammakka's 'Kumkuma Bharina' is at Chilakala Gutta.

text:
Question: What is the schedule for the 4-day Jathara?
Answer: Day 1 (Wednesday) — Secret morning pujas at Kannepally; evening 6:00 PM: Saralamma brought to Medaram Gaddhe via Jampanna Vaagu; over 3 million devotees. Day 2 (Thursday) — Edurukolla Ghattam (bamboo-stick ritual); evening 6:00 PM: Sammakka brought from Chilakala Gutta to gaddhe; SP fires 3 gunshots to inaugurate the bali. Day 3 (Friday) — Main day: devotees take Punya Snanams in Jampanna Vaagu; main darshan of Sammakka and Saralamma; offerings of Bangaram, Odi Biyyam, sarees, turmeric, vermilion, rice, cloth. Day 4 (Saturday) — Final darshan; afternoon Ammavarlu Vana Pravesham (return to forest at ~6:00 PM); the 4-day Jathara concludes with religious chants.

text:
Question: How big is the Sammakka Saralamma Jathara?
Answer: The 2026 Jathara drew an estimated 80 lakh devotees on the first two days alone, with the full 4-day total expected to reach nearly 3 crore. The Telangana government deployed 21 government departments, 42,027 personnel, ~9,000 police officers, hundreds of CCTV cameras, 2 drone cameras, ~500 NSS volunteers from Kakatiya University, and TSRTC ran nearly 4,000 buses daily. The traffic jam can extend up to 60 km on the Warangal highway. It is the largest tribal religious gathering in the world and the second-largest religious gathering in India after the Kumbh Mela.

text:
Question: Who are Sammakka and Saralamma?
Answer: Per tribal tradition, goddess Sammakka was born in the 13th century, found as a newborn emitting enormous light amid tigers, adopted by the Koya tribe head. She married Pagididda Raju, a feudatory tribal chief of the Kakatiyas, and had 2 daughters (Sarakka/Saralamma, Nagulamma) and 1 son (Jampanna). She led a tribal revolt against the unjust Kakatiya tax during a drought. Jampanna, her son, died fighting the Kakatiyan Army at a stream (now Jampanna Vagu). Per legend, Sammakka's curse caused the Kakatiya decline. Saralamma is installed in a temple at Kannepally; Sammakka is at Chilakala Gutta in the form of a 'Kumkuma Bharina' (vermilion form).

text:
Question: What is the Jampanna Vagu?
Answer: Jampanna Vagu is a tributary of the River Godavari that flows through the Eturnagaram Wildlife Sanctuary near Medaram. It is named after the tribal warrior Jampanna (Sammakka's son), who died fighting the Kakatiyan Army in that stream. The water is still reddish in colour — tribally believed to be marked with his blood (scientifically attributed to the soil composition). A holy dip (Punya Snanam) in the red waters is central to the Jathara experience. The Jampanna Vagu bridge crosses the stream.

text:
Question: What is Bangaram and how is it offered?
Answer: Bangaram is the local name for jaggery (bellam) — symbolic of gold. It is the most important offering in the Sammakka Sarakka Jathara. Devotees offer jaggery of a quantity equal to their body weight to the goddesses. The offering is part of the Mokubadulu (vow fulfilment) tradition. Other offerings include Odi Biyyam (sacred rice, by women), sarees, turmeric, vermilion, rice and cloth.

text:
Question: What should I wear and bring for the Jathara?
Answer: Wear traditional attire — men in dhoti (often shirtless at the gaddelu per tribal convention); women in sarees (which is also a principal offering). Carry water, light food, comfortable footwear (which you'll remove at the gaddelu and Jampanna Vagu), a towel for the holy dip, and jaggery (Bangaram) of a quantity equal to your body weight for the principal offering. There are no ATMs or banks at Medaram — carry sufficient cash. Be prepared for massive crowds (up to 40 lakh on Day 3).

text:
Question: What is the connection between the Jathara and Sammakka's curse on the Kakatiyas?
Answer: Per tribal tradition, goddess Sammakka's curse is said to have caused the gradual decline and death of the Kakatiya rule. After Sammakka and her daughter led the tribal revolt against the unjust Kakatiya tax during a drought, and after her son Jampanna died fighting the Kakatiyan Army at Jampanna Vagu, the Kakatiya empire gradually declined. The Jathara commemorates this tribal resistance and the sacrifice of Sammakka, Saralamma and Jampanna. It is a major assertion of tribal cultural identity and the memory of the 13th-century tribal revolt against the unjust Kakatiya rule.

text: Alternate names: Surendrapuri Mythological Awareness Center Kunda Satyanarayana Kaladhamam Kunda Satyanarayana Kala Dhamam Surendrapuri Mythological Theme Park Surendrapuri Religious Complex Surendrapuri Museum Alternate spellings: Surendrapuri Kunda Satyanarayana Kaladhamam Kunda Satyanarayana Kala Dhamam Surendra Puri Surendrapuri Mythological Awareness Center Presiding deity: Panchamukha Hanuman (16-foot black-stone idol from Kanchi; 5 faces — Vanara, Narasimha, Garuda, Varaha, Hayagreeva) — also venerated as a protective avatara who killed the 5 bees that hid Mahi Ravan's life. Lord Venkateswara and Goddess Lakshmi are also worshipped in the Panchamukha Hanumadeeswara Devasthanam. Other deities: Lord Shiva — Panchamukha Parameswara (Mahashivalinga similar to Pasupatinath, Nepal) Lord Nagakoteeswara Swamy (101-foot Shivalinga atop Nagadri Hill, encircled by Kaalasarpa) 10 million small Shivalingas (made of anthill mud) at the Nagakoti shrine Navagrahas (9 planetary deities — Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Rahu, Ketu — each in dedicated temples with their consorts and vahanas) 60-foot double-sided statue of Panchamukha Hanuman and Panchamukha Shiva at the entrance Life-size replicas of 100+ famous Indian temple deities (Tirumala Balaji, Madurai Meenakshi, Kashi Viswanath, Shirdi Saibaba, Rameswaram, Jagannath Puri, Golden Temple Amritsar, Somnath, Kedarnath, Guruvayur, etc.) Surendrapuri — Kunda Satyanarayana Kaladhamam, located at the foothills of Yadagirigutta in Yadadri-Bhuvanagiri District, Telangana, is India's first mythological theme park and religious tourism destination, spread over 17 acres. Opened to the public in May 2003 by Sri Kunda Satyanarayana (in memory of his late son Surendra), the complex features 3,000+ sculptures across a 3-km pathway, organised into four categories: Temples of India (life-size replicas of 100+ famous Indian temples), Epics of India (Ramayana, Mahabharata, Bhagavata, Buddha Charita), Puranas (Ksheera Sagara Madhanam, Gajendra Moksham, Padmavyuham, Kurukshetra War, etc.), and Saptalokas (the 7 celestial worlds — Brahmalok, Vishnulok, Shivalok, Nagalok, Indralok, Narakalok/Yamalok, Patalalok). The complex also houses the Panchamukha Hanumadeeswara Devasthanam (16-foot black-stone Panchamukha Hanuman from Kanchi + Mahashivalinga similar to Pasupatinath Nepal), 9 Navagraha Temples (each planet with its consort and vahana in dedicated temples), Nagakoti (a 101-foot Shivalinga atop Nagadri Hill encircled by Kaalasarpa with 10 million small anthill-mud Shivalingas), and Surendrapuri's iconic 60-foot double-sided Panchamukha Hanuman-Shiva statue at the entrance. ~60 km from Hyderabad; 10 km from Bhuvanagiri Railway Station; 2 km from Yadadri Bus Terminal. Entry: Adult ₹350, Child (5–10 yrs) ₹300, below 5 years free. Open daily 9 AM – 5:30 PM (visiting 9 AM – 7 PM).

text: section: Founder & Personal Motivation content: Surendrapuri was conceptualized and built by Sri Kunda Satyanarayana, who was born in a small village near Khammam (Telangana) in an agricultural family whose modest means did not allow him to pursue a formal higher education. The sudden passing away of his youngest son, Surendra Babu, aroused in Sri Satyanarayana a desire to build something to keep his memory alive. The idea of a mythological park seemed apt due to his deep abiding love for Indian culture and traditions. He was confronted by daunting challenges — advancing age, huge project costs, and the dissuasion of friends and associates. All the deterrents only served to firm his resolve. At the age of 70, when people have generally retired, he worked doubly hard to bring his dream project to life. After over a decade of dedicated hard work and single-minded commitment, Surendrapuri took concrete shape. Today it stands as a testament to one man's vision, determination and never-say-die attitude. foundation year: Surendrapuri opened to the public in May 2003; the Kunda Satyanarayana Kaladhamam (the mythological museum) was inaugurated in February 2009 by the then-Governor of Andhra Pradesh, Narayan Dutt Tiwari founders: Sri Kunda Satyanarayana (born in a small village near Khammam, agricultural family; built the park in memory of his son Surendra Babu who passed away suddenly) legends: Sri Kunda Satyanarayana lost his youngest son Surendra Babu suddenly, which motivated him to build a memorial that would keep his son's memory alive. The idea of a mythological park came to him due to his deep abiding love for Indian culture and traditions. At age 70, when most people have retired, Satyanarayana worked doubly hard to bring his dream project to life, after facing dissuasion from friends and associates. After over a decade of dedication, Surendrapuri was completed and opened in May 2003.

text: Surendrapuri does not have a traditional Sthala Puranam as it is a modern mythological theme park and religious tourism destination. The site's sacred character is derived from the 100+ life-size replicas of India's most revered temples (including Tirumala Balaji, Madurai Meenakshi, Kashi Viswanath, Rameswaram, Jagannath Puri, Golden Temple Amritsar, Somnath, Kedarnath, Guruvayur), the sculpted depictions of key events from the Ramayana, Mahabharata, Bhagavata, the life of Buddha, and key events from the Puranas (Ksheera Sagara Madhanam / churning of the ocean, Gajendra Moksham, Padmavyuham, Kurukshetra War, etc.), and the 7 celestial Saptalokas (Brahmalok, Vishnulok, Shivalok, Nagalok, Indralok, Narakalok/Yamalok, Patalalok). The complex also houses the Panchamukha Hanumadeeswara Devasthanam (the protective avatara of Hanuman who killed the 5 bees that hid Mahi Ravan's life), the 101-foot Nagakoti Shivalinga (with 10 million small anthill-mud Shivalingas for Naga Dosha, Kuja Dosha and Kaalasarpa Dosha remedies), and the 9 Navagraha Temples. Surendrapuri is named after Sri Kunda Satyanarayana's son Surendra Babu, and the Kaladhamam is named after Sri Satyanarayana himself.
